'''''Cascabela thevetia''''' ([[Synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''Thevetia peruviana'') is a species of [[poisonous plant]] in the dogbane family [[Apocynaceae]], native throughout [[Mexico]] and [[Central America]] and cultivated widely as an ornamental. It is a relative of ''[[Nerium oleander]]'' and thus is known by the common name '''yellow oleander'''.

==Etymology==
The name derives from the Spanish words ''cascabel'', ''cascavel'', or ''cascabela'', which can refer to a small bell, a snake's rattle, or a [[rattlesnake]] itself.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Quattrocchi|first1=Umberto|title=CRC World Dictionary of Plant Names: Common Names, Scientific Names, Eponyms, Synonyms, and Etymology|date=1999|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=978-0-8493-2673-8|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=A68qyOyhOdkC&q=Cascabela+etymology&pg=PA448|language=en}}</ref> The name may also allude to the plant's toxicity being comparable to the venom of a rattlesnake. The specific epithet ''thevetia'' commemorates [[André de Thevet]] (1516–1590), a French Franciscan priest and explorer who explored Brazil and Guiana<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cascabela thevetia - Plant Finder|url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=276151|access-date=2021-12-22|website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref> (where the plant is known as ''chapéu-de-napoleão'', i.e. "Napoleon's hat").

==Description==
''Cascabela thevetia'' is an evergreen [[tropical shrub]] or small tree. Its leaves are willow-like, linear-lanceolate, and glossy green in color. They are covered in a waxy coating to reduce water loss (typical of oleanders). Its stem is green and turns silver/gray as it ages.<ref name="kemper">{{cite web | url = http://www.mobot.org/gardeninghelp/plantfinder/Plant.asp?code=A551 | title = ''Thevetia peruvians'' | publisher = Missouri Botanical Garden | access-date = 2011-04-19 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20041209235844/http://www.mobot.org/gardeninghelp/plantfinder/Plant.asp?code=A551 | archive-date = 2004-12-09 }}</ref> Flowers bloom from summer to fall. The long, funnel-shaped, sometimes fragrant yellow (less commonly apricot, sometimes white) flowers are in few-flowered terminal clusters.<ref name="kemper"/> Its fruit is deep red-black in color, encasing a large seed that bears some resemblance to a 'Chinese lucky nut.'{{clarify|what's that?|date=May 2014}}

''Cascabela thevetia'' is effectively drought-resistant and tolerant to high temperatures, and hence has been naturalized in various semi-arid regions of India.{{citation needed|date=April 2025}}

==Religious importance==
Its bright yellow flowers are used for religious purposes in India, including the worship practices of Hindu devotees.{{citation needed|date=November 2024}}

==Toxicity==
All parts of the ''C. thevetia'' plant are toxic to most vertebrates as they contain [[cardiac glycoside]]s. Many cases of intentional and accidental poisoning of humans are known.<ref>{{cite journal| title=Oleander toxicity: an examination of human and animal toxic exposures| author= Shannon D. Langford| author2= Paul J. Boor| name-list-style= amp | doi=10.1016/0300-483X(95)03296-R | journal=Toxicology| pmid=8619248 | volume=109| issue=1| year=1996| pages= 1–13| bibcode= 1996Toxgy.109....1L}}</ref> Case reports have identified Tecojote root supplements as a source of accidental ingestion of yellow oleander.

The main toxins are the [[cardenolide]]s [[thevetin A]] and [[thevetin B]]; others include [[peruvoside]], [[neriifolin]], [[thevetoxin]] and [[ruvoside]].<ref>{{cite journal| vauthors = Bose TK, Basu RK, Biswas B, De JN, Majumdar BC, Datta S | year=1999| title=Cardiovascular effects of yellow oleander ingestion| journal=J Indian Med Assoc |volume=97 |issue=10 |pages=407–410 |pmid=10638101}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal| vauthors = Kohls S, Scholz-Böttcher BM, Teske J, Zark P, Rullkötter J | year=2012 |title=Cardiac glycosides from Yellow Oleander (Thevetia peruviana) seeds |journal=Phytochemistry |pages=114–27 |doi=10.1016/j.phytochem.2011.11.019 |pmid=22196940 |volume=75| bibcode=2012PChem..75..114K }}</ref> These cardenolides are not destroyed by drying or heating and are very similar to [[digoxin]] from ''[[Digitalis purpurea]]''. They produce [[gastric]] upset and [[cardiotoxic]] effects, such as an [[bradycardia|abnormally slow heart rate]], EKG abnormalities (scooped ST segments), and [[hyperkalemia|abnormally high levels of potassium in the blood]]. Antidotes include [[atropine]] and [[digoxin immune fab]]s (antibodies), and treatment may include oral administration of [[activated charcoal]].<ref>{{cite journal | author = Rajapakse S. | title = Management of yellow oleander poisoning | journal = Clinical Toxicology | year = 2009 | volume = 47 | issue = 3 | pages = 206–212 | doi=10.1080/15563650902824001 | pmid=19306191| s2cid = 37334350 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author = Roberts D.M. | author2 = Southcott E. | author3 = Potter J.M. | author4 = Roberts M.S. | author5 = Eddleston M. | author6 = Buckley N.A. | title = Pharmacokinetics of digoxin cross-reacting substances in patients with acute yellow oleander (Thevetia peruviana) poisoning, including the effect of activated charcoal | journal = Therapeutic Drug Monitoring | year = 2006 | volume = 28  | issue = 6 | pages = 784–792 | doi=10.1097/ftd.0b013e31802bfd69| pmid = 17164695 | pmc = 2296884 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author = Bandara V. | author2 = Weinstein S.A. | author3 = White J. | author4 = Eddleston M. | title = A review of the natural history, toxinology, diagnosis and clinical management of Nerium oleander (common oleander) and Thevetia peruviana (yellow oleander) poisoning | journal = Toxicon | year = 2010 | volume = 56 | issue = 3 | pages = 273–281 | doi=10.1016/j.toxicon.2010.03.026 | pmid=20438743| bibcode = 2010Txcn...56..273B }}</ref> Ovine polyclonal anti-digitoxin Fab fragment antibody (DigiTAb; Therapeutic Antibodies Inc.) can be used to treat ''T. peruviana'' poisoning, but in many countries the cost is prohibitively high.<ref>{{cite journal | author = M. Eddleston | author2 = S. Rajapakse | author3 = Rajakanthan, S. Jayalath | author4 = L. Sjöström | author5 = W. Santharaj | name-list-style = amp | title = Anti-digoxin Fab fragments in cardiotoxicity induced by ingestion of yellow oleander: a randomised controlled trial | journal = Lancet | volume = 355 | issue = 9208 | year = 2000 | pages = 967–972 | doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(00)90014-X| pmid = 10768435 | s2cid = 2095538 |display-authors=etal}}</ref>

A few bird species are, however, known to feed on them without any ill effects. These include [[sunbirds]], [[Asian koel]], [[red-whiskered bulbul]], [[white-browed bulbul]], [[red-vented bulbul]], [[brahminy myna]], [[common myna]] and [[common grey hornbill]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Kannan, R|year=1991|title=Koels feeding on the yellow oleander.|journal=Blackbuck|volume=7|issue=2|page=48}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Krishnan, M|author-link=Madhaviah Krishnan|year=1952|title= Koels (''Eudynamis scolopaceus'') eating the poisonous fruit of the Yellow Oleander.|journal=J. Bombay Nat. Hist. Soc. |volume=50|issue=4|pages=943–945}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Raj, PJ Sanjeeva |year=1963|title=Additions to the list of birds eating the fruit of Yellow Oleander (''Thevetia neriifolia'' ).|journal=J. Bombay Nat. Hist. Soc.|volume=60|issue=2|pages=457–458}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Birds eating poisonous fruit of Yellow Oleander (''Thevetia neriifolia'')| journal=J. Bombay Nat. Hist. Soc.|page=639| volume=56|issue=3|author=Raj, P J Sanjeeva|year=1959}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author= Neelakantan, KK |year=1953| title= Common Grey Hornbill (''Tockus birostris'') eating fruits of the Yellow Oleander (''Thevetia neriifolia'')| journal= J. Bombay Nat. Hist. Soc.|volume=51|issue=3|page=738}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author= Rajasingh, Simon G|author2= Rajasingh, Irene V |year=1970 |title= Birds and mammals eating the fruits of Yellow Oleander (''Thevetia peruviana'') |journal= J. Bombay Nat. Hist. Soc. |volume=67|issue=3|pages=572–573}}</ref>

In South India and in Sri Lanka, swallowing the seeds of ''Thevetia peruviana''<ref>[http://www.inchem.org/documents/pims/plant/thevetia.htm#SectionTitle:1.1%20Scientific%20name Thevetia peruviana]</ref> (Kaneru කණේරු (Sinhala), Manjal arali (Tamil)) is one of the preferred methods for suicides in villages where they are grown in abundance.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://academic.oup.com/qjmed/article/92/9/483/1520521|title=Management of acute yellow oleander poisoning| author=M. Eddleston, D.A. Warrell| publisher=QJM: An International Journal of Medicine| date=1999-09-01| access-date=2018-02-20}}</ref>

Extracts from ''C. thevetia'' are reported to possess antispermatogenic activity in rats.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite journal|vauthors=Gupta R, Kachhawa JB, Gupta RS, Sharma AK, Sharma MC, Dobhal MP |title=Phytochemical evaluation and antispermatogenic activity of Thevetia peruviana methanol extract in male albino rats |journal=Hum Fertil (Camb) |date=March 2011 |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=53–59 |doi=10.3109/14647273.2010.542230|pmid=21466267 |s2cid=24757302 }}</ref>

In 2023, the US [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) and [[Food and Drug Administration]] (FDA) reported on weight loss supplements which had substituted ''[[Crataegus mexicana]]'' and ''[[Aleurites moluccanus]]'' for ''C. thevetia'', following multiple hospitalizations.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Berland |first1=Noah |last2=Kababick |first2=James |last3=Santos |first3=Cynthia |last4=Calello |first4=Diane P. |date=15 September 2023 |title=Notes from the Field: Online Weight Loss Supplements Labeled as Tejocote (Crataegus mexicana) Root, Substituted with Yellow Oleander (Cascabela thevetia) — United States, 2022 |url=https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/wr/mm7237a3.htm |journal=[[Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report]] |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] |volume=72 |issue=37 |pages=1016–1017|doi=10.15585/mmwr.mm7237a3 |pmid=37708076 |pmc=10511264 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=8 September 2023 |title=The FDA Expands Warning to Consumers About Toxic Yellow Oleander Purported to be Nuez de la India in Certain Botanical Weight Loss Products |url=https://www.fda.gov/food/alerts-advisories-safety-information/fda-expands-warning-consumers-about-toxic-yellow-oleander-purported-be-nuez-de-la-india-certain |access-date=2 October 2023 |website=[[Food and Drug Administration]]}}</ref>

==Uses==
;Cultivation
''Cascabela thevetia'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]] and is commonly planted as a large flowering shrub or small [[ornamental tree]] in gardens and parks in temperate climates. In frost-prone areas it is usually a container plant and in the winter season is brought inside a [[greenhouse]] or home as a [[house plant]]. It tolerates most soils and is drought-tolerant.<ref name="kemper"/>

;Biological pest control
The plant's toxins have been tested in experiments for uses as a [[biological pest control]]. ''T. peruviana'' seed oil was used to make a 'paint' with antifungal, antibacterial and anti-termite properties.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Kareru P.G. | author2 = Keriko J.M. | author3 = Kenji G.M. | author4 = Gachanja A.N. | title = Anti-termite and antimicrobial properties of paint made from ''Thevetia peruviana'' (Pers.) Schum. oil extract | journal = African Journal of Pharmacy and Pharmacology | year = 2010 | volume = 4 | issue = 2 | pages = 87–89}}</ref>
